readings.c1s1:
following tests. If <math>\sqrt[n]{u_n}</math> approaches a limit <math>l</math> as <math>n</math> is indefinitely increased, <math>\Sigma u_n</math> will converge if <math>l</math> is less than unity and will diverge if <math>l</math> is greater than unity (Cauchy's test); if <math>u_{n+1}/u_n</math> approaches a limit <math>l</math> as <math>n</math> is indefinitely increased, <math>\Sigma u_n</math> will converge if <math>l</math> is less than unity and diverge if <math>l</math> is greater than unity (D'Alembert's test). Nothing is settled when the limit <math>l</math> is unity, except in the case when <math>l</math> remains greater than unity as it approaches unity. The series then diverges. It may be remarked that if <math>u_{n+1}/u_n</math> approaches a limit and <math>\sqrt[n]{u_n}</math> approaches a limit, the two limits are the same. The choice of the more useful test to apply to a particular series depends on its form.

In the case in which <math>u_{n+1}/u_n</math> approaches unity remaining constantly less than unity, J. L. Raabe and J. M. C. Duhamel have given the following further criterion. Write <math>u_n/u_{n+1} = 1 + \alpha_n</math>, where <math>\alpha_n</math> is positive and approaches zero as <math>n</math> is indefinitely increased. If <math>n\alpha_n</math> approaches a limit <math>l</math>, the series converges for <math>l > 1</math> and diverges for <math>l < 1</math>. For <math>l = 1</math> nothing is settled except for the case where <math>l</math> remains constantly less than unity as it approaches it; in this case the series diverges.

If <math>f(n)</math> is positive and decreases as <math>n</math> increases, the series <math>\Sigma f(n)</math> is convergent or divergent with the series <math>\Sigma a^n f(a^n)</math> where <math>a</math> is any number <math>>2</math> (Cauchy's condensation test). By means of this theorem we can show that the series whose general terms are
{{block center|<math>\frac{1}{n^\alpha}, \frac{1}{n(\text{l}n)^\alpha}, \frac{1}{n\text{l}n(\text{l}^2n)^\alpha}, \frac{1}{n\text{l}n\text{l}^2n(\text{l}^3n)^\alpha} \dots,</math>}}

where <math>\text{l}n</math> denotes <math>\log n</math>, <math>\text{l}^2n</math> denotes <math>\log\cdot\log n</math>, <math>\text{l}^3n</math> denotes <math>\log\log\log n</math>, and so on, are convergent if <math>\alpha > 1</math> and divergent if <math>\alpha = \text{or} < 1</math>.

By comparison with these series, a sequence of criteria, known as the logarithm criteria, has been established by De Morgan and J. L. Bertrand. A. De Morgan's form is as follows: writing <math>u_n = 1/\phi(n)</math>, put <math>p_0 = x\phi'(x)/\phi(x)</math>, <math>p_1 = (p_0 - 1)\text{l}x</math>, <math>p_2 = (p_1 - 1)\text{l}^2x</math>, <math>p_3 = (p_2 - 1)\text{l}_3x, \dots</math> where <math>\text{l}^rx</math> denotes <math>\log\log\log\dots x</math>. If the limit, when <math>x</math> is infinite, of the first of the functions <math>p_0, p_1, p_2, \dots</math>, whose limit is not unity, is greater than unity the series is convergent, if less than unity it is divergent.

In Bertrand's form we take the series of functions
{{block center|<math>\text{l}\frac{1}{u_n}/\text{l}n,\ \text{l}\frac{1}{nu_n}/\text{l}^2n,\ \text{l}\frac{1}{nu_n\text{l}n}/\text{l}^3n, \dots</math>}}
If the limit, when <math>n</math> is infinite, of the first of these functions, whose limit is not unity, is greater than unity the series is convergent, if less than unity it is divergent. Other forms of these criteria may be found in Chrystal's ''Algebra'', vol. ii.

Though sufficient to test such series as occur in ordinary mathematics, it is possible to construct series for which they entirely fail. It follows that in a convergent series not only must we have <math>\text{Lt}\,u_n = 0</math> but also <math>\text{Lt}\,nu_n = 0</math>, <math>\text{Lt}\,n\text{l}nu_n = 0</math>, &c. Abel has, however, shown that no function <math>\phi(n)</math> can exist such that the series <math>\Sigma u_n</math> is convergent or divergent as <math>\text{Lt}\,\phi(n)u_n</math> is or is not zero.

Similarly two or more absolutely convergent series may be multiplied together thus <math>(u_1 + u_2 + u_3 + \dots)\ (v_1 + v_2 + v_3 + \dots) = u_1v_1 + (u_1v_2 + u_2v_1) + (u_1v_3 + u_2v_2 + u_3v_1) + \dots</math>, and the resulting series is absolutely convergent and its sum is the product of the sums of the two series. This was shown by Cauchy, who also showed that the series <math>\Sigma w_n</math>, where <math>w_n = u_1v_n + u_2v_{n-1} +</math>

A striking instance is furnished by the series <math>1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{4}}+\dots</math> which is convergent, while its square <math>1-\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}}+\left(\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}+\frac{1}{2}\right)-\dots</math> may be shown to be divergent. F. K. L. Mertens has shown that a sufficient condition is that one of the two series should be absolutely convergent, and Abel has shown that if <math>\Sigma w_n</math> converges at all, it converges to the product of <math>\Sigma u_n</math> and <math>\Sigma v_n</math>. But more properly the multiplication of two series gives rise to a double series of which the general term is <math>u_mv_n</math>.

{{block center|<math>\dots u_{-m}+\dots+u_{-2}+u_{-1}+u_0+u_1+u_2+\dots+u_n+\dots</math>}}
Such a series may be absolutely convergent and the sum is then independent of the order of the terms and is equal to the sums of the two series <math>u_0+u_1+u_2+\dots</math> and <math>u_{-1}+u_{-2}+\dots</math>, but, if not absolutely convergent, the expression has no definite meaning until it is explained in what manner the terms are intended to be grouped together; for instance, the expression may be used to denote the foregoing sum of two series, or to denote the series <math>u_0+(u_1+u_{-1})+(u_2+u_{-2})+\dots</math>, and the sum may have different values, or there may be no sum, accordingly. So, if the series be taken to denote the limit of <math>(u_0+u_1+\dots+u_n)+(u_{-1}+u_{-}+\dots+u_{-m})</math>, where <math>n</math> and <math>m</math> are each of them ultimately

14. It is easy to see that, if each of the terms <math>u_{m,n}</math> is positive and the series is convergent for any particular form of boundary, it will be convergent for any other form of boundary, and the sum will be the same in each case. Suppose that in the first case the boundary is the curve <math>f_1(x,\ y) = \text{T}</math>. Draw any other boundary <math>f_2(x,\ y) = \text{T}'</math>. Wholly within this we can draw a curve <math>f_1(x,\ y) = \text{T}_1</math> of the first family, and wholly outside it we can draw a second curve of the first family, <math>f_1(x,\ y) = \text{T}_2</math>. The sum of all the points within <math>f_2(x,\ y) = \text{T}'</math> lies between the sum of all the points within <math>f_1(x,\ y) = \text{T}_1</math> and the sum of all the points within <math>f_1(x,\ y) = \text{T}_2</math>. It therefore tends to the common limit to which these two last sums tend. The sum is therefore independent of the form of the boundary. Such a series is said to be absolutely convergent, and similarly a doubly infinite series of positive and negative terms is absolutely convergent when the series formed by taking all its terms positively is convergent.

15. It is readily seen that when the series is not absolutely convergent the sum will depend on the form of the boundary. Consider the case in which <math>m</math> and <math>n</math> are always positive, and the boundary is the rectangle formed by <math>x = m</math>, <math>y = n</math>, and the axes. Let the sum within this rectangle be <math>\text{S}_{m,n}</math>. This may have a limit when we first make <math>n</math> infinite and then <math>m</math>; it may have a limit when we first make <math>m</math> infinite and then <math>n</math>, but the limits are not necessarily the same; or there may be no limit in either of these cases but a limit depending on the ratio of <math>m</math> to <math>n</math>, that is to say, on the shape of the rectangle.

When the product of two series is arranged as a doubly infinite series, summing for the rectangular boundary <math>x = \alpha\text{T}</math>, <math>y = \beta\text{T}</math> we obtain the product of the sums of the series. When we arrange the double series in the form <math>u_1v_1 + (u_1v_2 + u_2v_1) + \dots</math> we are summing over the triangle bounded by the axes and the straight line <math>x + y = \text{T}</math>, and the results are not necessarily the same if the terms are not all positive. For full particulars concerning multiple series the reader may consult E. Goursat, ''Cours d'analyse'', vol. i.; G. Chrystal, ''Algebra'',

vol. ii.; or T. J. I'A. Bromwich, ''The Theory of Infinite Series.''

16. In the series so far considered the terms are actual numbers, or, at least, if the terms are functions of a variable, we have considered the convergency only when that variable has an assigned value. In the case, however, of a series <math>u_1(z)+u_2(z)+\dots</math>, where <math>u_1(z)</math>, <math>u_2(z)</math>,… are single-valued continuous functions of the general complex variable <math>z</math>, if the series converges for any value of <math>z</math>, in general it converges for all values of <math>z</math>, whose representative points lie within a certain area called the "domain of convergence" and within this area defines a function which we may call <math>\text{S}(z)</math>. It might be supposed that <math>\text{S}(z)</math> was necessarily a continuous function of <math>z</math>, but this is not the case. G. G. Stokes (1847) and P. L. Seidel (1848) independently discovered that in the neighbourhood of a point of discontinuity the convergence is infinitely slow and thence arises the notion of ''uniform'' and ''non-uniform'' convergence.

17. If for any value of <math>z</math> the series <math>u_1(z)+u_2(z)+\dots</math> converges it is possible to find an integer <math>n</math> such that <math>|\text{S}(z)-\text{S}_n(z)|<\epsilon</math>, <math>|\text{S}(z)-\text{S}_{n+1}(z)|<\epsilon,\dots</math>, where <math>\epsilon</math> is any arbitrarily assigned positive quantity, however small. For a given <math>\epsilon</math> the least value of <math>n</math> will vary throughout any region from point to point of that region. It may, however, be possible to find an integer <math>\nu</math> which is a superior limit to all the values of <math>n</math> in that region, and we thus have, throughout this region, <math>|\text{S}(z)-\text{S}_\nu(z)|<\epsilon</math>, <math>|\text{S}(z)-\text{S}_{\nu+1}(z)|<\epsilon\dots</math> where <math>z</math> is any point in the region and <math>\nu</math> is a finite integer depending only on <math>\epsilon</math> and not on <math>z</math>.

In a singly infinite series we have a general term <math>u_n</math>, where <math>n</math> is an integer positive in the case of an ordinary series, and positive or negative in the case of a back-and-forwards series. {{block center|<math>u_{0,0},\ u_{0,1},\ u_{0,2}, \dots</math>}}

{{block center|<math>u_{1,0},\ u_{1,1},\ u_{1,2}, \dots</math>}}

{{block center|<math>\vdots \qquad \vdots \qquad \vdots</math>}}

or they may be each of them positive or negative. The latter is the more general supposition, and includes the former, since <math>u_{m,n}</math> may <math>=0</math>, for <math>m</math> or <math>n</math> each or either of them negative. To attach a definite meaning to the notion of a sum, we may regard <math>m</math>, <math>n</math> as the rectangular coordinates of a point in a plane; if <math>m</math> and <math>n</math> are each positive we attend only to the positive quadrant of the plane, but otherwise to the whole plane. It may, however, be possible to find an integer <math>\nu</math> which is a superior limit to all the values of <math>n</math> in that region, and we thus have, throughout this region, <math>|\text{S}(z)-\text{S}_\nu(z)|<\epsilon</math>, <math>|\text{S}(z)-\text{S}_{\nu+1}(z)|<\epsilon\dots</math> where <math>z</math> is any point in the region and <math>\nu</math> is a finite integer depending only on <math>\epsilon</math> and not on <math>z</math>.<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
